rv.q: Are we likely to see a more enthralling play in the West End this year? I very much doubt it.
It’s hard to think when the Royal Court last staged a play that felt so dangerous, or one so spectacularly good.
Here in one evening is the case for the stage.
An incisive, powerhouse production, Giant makes us reconsider that age-old dilemma - can we separate the artist from the art?
Giant shows a necessary bravery in taking it on.

What is really shocking and impressive about Nicholas Hytner's production is not that Dahl is exposed – this is a matter of public record. Instead, it's the fact that the play is a violent, incendiary provocation.
Giant ultimately lacks tension, because it’s clear from the start that Dahl is deeply but lazily prejudiced, with no intention of changing.
Certainly Rosenblatt casts him in this cogent, uncomfortable play as a man who always has the last laugh.
As emotions run hot, characters confront one another with some gasp-inducingly savage lines , but the most shocking moments come when Dahl’s public statements are quoted verbatim.
It’s a play that doesn’t quite decide where it stands in that argument about whether you can loathe the man and admire the art – but thanks to Lithgow, it compels while it is making it.

For all the fine talk of separating the art from the artist, it’s hard to escape the discomforting conclusion that Dahl was so good at writing about hatefulness and cruelty precisely because he was, in some respects, a hateful and cruel man.
Giant is an extraordinary piece of new writing, and I couldn't be more honoured to be part of bringing this fascinating, knotty, complicated, and unafraid piece to audiences for the first time.
A flawed play then, but one that at least tries to address thorny key issues of the day in politics and art.

cn.t: Critics largely praise *Giant* as a gripping, thought-provoking drama, with Lithgow's towering portrayal of Dahl earning near-universal acclaim. Some find the script uneven, but Hytner's direction keeps it compelling.
